title: AP Cybersecurity
summary: Practise defensive risk analysis, access control and evidence-based detection across five units.
frameworkNote: Checked against the new five-unit 2026-27 course on 15 October 2026. All scenarios are fictional defensive exercises. They require no probing, credential collection or changes to real systems. Text practice does not replace supervised labs, authorised hands-on work or required course assessments.

modules.title: Separate identity, authentication and risk
modules.focus: Unit 1: recognise social engineering and choose layered controls.
explanation: Identification names a claimed identity; authentication checks evidence supporting that claim; authorisation determines what the verified identity may do. A strong login alone does not justify unrestricted access. Risk combines the likelihood and impact of a threat acting on a vulnerability.

Social engineering exploits trust, urgency or authority. A message’s familiar display name is not sufficient proof of origin. Use an independently known channel to verify unusual requests, report suspicious messages through approved processes and avoid sharing credentials. Multiple factors should come from different factor categories rather than two versions of the same secret.

workedExample.prompt: A fictional message asks a student to send a password immediately to avoid account closure.
steps: Identify urgency and a request for a secret as warning signs.
Do not reply with credentials; verify through the school’s known support route and report the message.

misconception.claim: Two passwords are two independent authentication factors.
misconception.correction: They are both knowledge factors; a second factor should use a different category.

questions.prompt: Which is authorisation: checking a login code or deciding whether a user may edit records?
questions.hint: Distinguish identity proof from permission.
questions.answer: Deciding whether the user may edit records is authorisation.

questions.prompt: Why use a known support address instead of the message’s link?
questions.hint: Consider who supplied the destination.
questions.answer: The message may supply an attacker-controlled destination; an independently known route avoids trusting that instruction.

questions.hint: Login and record access are separate decisions.
questions.prompt: A user can sign in but cannot view another learner’s feedback. Identify the control that should enforce this restriction and what it must check.
questions.answer: Authorisation must check that the signed-in identity has permission for that specific feedback record and requested action.
checkpoints: Bind the check to the requested record.
Include the operation and authenticated identity.
hints: Login and record access are separate decisions.
The resource owner or role matters at the moment of access.

questions.hint: Temporary does not mean harmless.
questions.prompt: A message asks for a one-time login code and claims urgent account repair. Give a safe verification response and explain why sharing the code is risky.
questions.answer: Do not send the code; contact support through a previously known official route. A login code can complete another party’s authentication attempt even though it is temporary.
checkpoints: Use an independent known support route.
Explain that the code can enable account access.
hints: Temporary does not mean harmless.
Do not use the message’s own contact details as independent confirmation.

notes.title: Reasoning through separate identity, authentication and risk
paragraphs: Identity states who an account claims to represent, authentication tests that claim, and authorisation determines which actions the authenticated account may perform. These are separate controls: successful login does not justify access to every record. Risk depends on the asset, plausible threat, weakness and potential impact rather than a dramatic label alone. Phishing attempts exploit trust, urgency or a misleading context, so verification should use an independently known route. Multifactor authentication combines distinct factor types; two passwords are still two examples of the same knowledge factor. Controls reduce risk but do not establish that every account action is legitimate.

workedExamples.prompt: A fictional portal accepts a student’s password and second factor, then rejects an attempt to edit the school timetable. Classify both decisions.
steps: The login checks authenticate the account by testing its credentials and additional factor.
The timetable rejection is authorisation: an authenticated student lacks the permission needed for that action.
workedExamples.conclusion: Authentication succeeded while the requested action was correctly denied by authorisation.

flashcards.back: The claimed identity using accepted evidence.
Which actions or resources that identity may access.
No; both are knowledge factors.

flashcards.front: Why verify a surprising request through a known channel?
flashcards.back: The request’s supplied contact route may belong to an impersonator.

modules.title: Protect spaces without overclaiming certainty
modules.focus: Unit 2: connect physical controls to threats and evidence.
explanation: Physical security protects people, equipment and information through access arrangements, environmental safeguards and monitoring. A locked room, visitor procedure and equipment inventory address different risks. Choose controls for a defined threat rather than collecting devices without a purpose.

Detection evidence requires interpretation. An access log records an event associated with a credential, not necessarily the identity of the person who used it. A missing asset may indicate theft, an undocumented move or an inventory error. Preserve records and follow the authorised reporting process before drawing conclusions.

workedExample.prompt: A fictional lab has an unlogged visitor and a missing laptop.
steps: Record the known facts and preserve relevant inventory and access records.
Report through the designated process and compare authorised moves before asserting who removed the device.

misconception.claim: An access-card event proves the named person was physically present.
misconception.correction: A credential may be shared, lost or misused; corroboration is needed.

questions.prompt: What risk does a visitor sign-in process address?
questions.hint: Think about accountability and permitted access.
questions.answer: It helps establish who was authorised to enter and when, supporting access control and later review.

questions.prompt: Why maintain an equipment inventory?
questions.hint: Compare expected and observed assets.
questions.answer: It provides a baseline for detecting missing or moved equipment and distinguishing documented changes from unexplained ones.

questions.hint: Only count records that can be matched to a specific asset.
questions.prompt: A room has 12 listed devices. Ten are present, one is signed out and one transfer record lacks a device identifier. How many are conclusively reconciled, and what remains?
questions.answer: Eleven are conclusively reconciled. The remaining device requires matching a valid identifier and transfer evidence; the incomplete record is not enough by itself.
checkpoints: Count ten present plus one documented loan.
Explain why the incomplete record cannot close the discrepancy.
hints: Only count records that can be matched to a specific asset.
Avoid treating a plausible explanation as verified.

questions.hint: A sequence of events is not proof of responsibility.
questions.prompt: A visitor log shows a person entered before a device was reported missing. Does this establish theft by that person? Explain an appropriate evidence-based response.
questions.answer: No. Timing alone does not establish who moved the device or whether it was stolen. Preserve the log, reconcile authorised movements and report the facts for review without unsupported accusation.
checkpoints: Reject the causal leap from timing.
Preserve and report evidence through the established process.
hints: A sequence of events is not proof of responsibility.
Keep observation separate from inference.

notes.title: Reasoning through protect spaces without overclaiming certainty
paragraphs: Physical security protects people, equipment and information by limiting opportunities for unauthorised access and by recording relevant events. An inventory identifies what should exist, where it belongs and who is responsible; it does not itself prevent theft. Visitor controls can establish an access record, but a sign-in entry alone does not prove what a person did inside. Combine prevention, detection and response measures according to the environment. When an item is missing, preserve accurate observations and report through the established process without accusing someone based only on proximity. Privacy and proportionality matter when collecting access or camera records.

workedExamples.prompt: A fictional lab inventory lists 25 laptops. A count finds 23, one documented repair shipment and one unexplained absence. State the reconciliation and next step.
steps: The 23 present plus one documented off-site unit account for 24 of 25; one remains unexplained.
Check authorised transfer records and report the discrepancy with device identifier, last confirmed location and time, preserving existing records.
workedExamples.conclusion: One laptop is unaccounted for; the evidence supports a discrepancy report, not an accusation.

flashcards.back: Expected assets, identifiers, locations and responsibility.

flashcards.front: Does a visitor log prove misconduct?
flashcards.back: No; it records access information with limits.
Comparing expected records with observed assets and documented movements.
They support reliable reconstruction and review.

nodes.label: Expected inventory
nodes.detail: Record uniquely identified equipment and authorised locations.

nodes.label: Observed count and movements

modules.title: Reason about segmentation and logs
explanation: Network segmentation separates groups of devices so that access can be controlled between them. A guest network should not automatically reach sensitive administrative systems. A firewall rule describes permitted or blocked traffic using defined criteria; its effectiveness depends on placement and the complete rule set.

Logs can reveal unusual patterns, but an alert is not proof of compromise. Compare source, destination, time and expected activity, then preserve the evidence for authorised review. These exercises use fictional descriptions only and do not require scanning or contacting any real network.

workedExample.prompt: A fictional school guest network can reach a records server it does not need.
steps: Identify the unnecessary path and the sensitive asset.
Propose a reviewed rule that blocks guest-to-records access while preserving required services, then verify it in an authorised test environment.

misconception.claim: A firewall makes every device behind it trustworthy.
misconception.correction: Allowed traffic and compromised internal devices still require layered controls.

questions.prompt: Why separate guest devices from administrative systems?
questions.hint: Consider unnecessary access and the impact of compromise.
questions.answer: Separation limits paths that guest devices do not need and can reduce the reach of an incident.
checkpoints: Does not promise total isolation without verification

questions.prompt: A log shows repeated denied connections. Does that prove a successful breach?
questions.hint: Distinguish attempted and completed actions.
questions.answer: No. It shows denied activity; investigation must determine its source, context and whether any access succeeded.

questions.hint: Use the event outcome literally.
questions.prompt: A log records 20 denied connections from a guest device to a server. What can be stated directly, and what cannot be concluded from this record alone?
questions.answer: The logging control recorded 20 denied attempts on the specified path. The record alone does not establish successful server access, malicious intent or the absence of other successful routes.
checkpoints: Identify an additional inference the log does not support.
hints: Use the event outcome literally.
One log source has a limited view.

questions.hint: Check what traffic can actually pass.
questions.prompt: A school separates guest and staff networks but accidentally permits guest access to the staff file service. Explain why separate network names alone are insufficient.
questions.answer: The required access restriction is not enforced on that path. Segmentation must be verified through actual permitted flows and access controls, not just labels or network names.
checkpoints: Recommend authorised testing against the intended access policy.
hints: Check what traffic can actually pass.
The security outcome depends on controls between groups.

notes.title: Reasoning through reason about segmentation and logs
paragraphs: Network segmentation separates systems so a problem in one area has fewer routes to affect others. A guest network may need internet access while having no business reason to reach administrative records; policy should describe the required flows before controls are tested. Logs record events from particular systems and can be incomplete because of retention, collection failures or clock differences. A denied connection shows an attempted path was blocked at that control, not that every related action failed or that a breach succeeded. Effective review correlates time, source, destination, action and outcome while respecting the limits of the evidence.

workedExamples.prompt: A fictional policy allows guest devices to reach the internet but denies access to a records server. A test records one blocked server connection and one successful internet connection. What is demonstrated?
steps: The observed cases match the intended deny and allow rules for those specific paths and times.
They do not prove every protocol, device or alternative route is controlled; additional authorised tests should cover the stated policy matrix.
workedExamples.conclusion: Two tested paths behaved as intended, with broader coverage still to be checked.

flashcards.front: What is segmentation intended to limit?
flashcards.back: Unnecessary connectivity and the spread of incidents.

flashcards.front: What should define a firewall test?
flashcards.back: The required source, destination, service and expected outcome.

flashcards.front: Does a denied log prove a successful intrusion?
flashcards.back: No.
Incorrect timestamps can distort event ordering across systems.

diagrams.description: Read the labelled connections together with the conditions stated at each node.

nodes.label: Required communication
nodes.detail: Document the flows each group actually needs.

nodes.label: Segmentation rules
nodes.detail: Permit necessary paths and restrict unnecessary ones.

nodes.label: Authorised verification
nodes.detail: Test representative allowed and denied paths and inspect evidence.

modules.title: Use a device baseline and safe response
modules.focus: Unit 4: manage updates, permissions and suspicious changes.
explanation: A secure device baseline records expected software, configuration and permitted access. Updates address known defects, while least privilege limits what ordinary accounts can change. Anti-malware tools add detection and prevention but cannot guarantee that every threat is found.

When a device behaves unexpectedly, preserve relevant information and follow the organisation’s response procedure. Unplanned deletion or repeated restarting can destroy useful evidence or complicate recovery. Distinguish a suspicious change from a confirmed compromise and escalate through the authorised support process.

workedExample.prompt: A fictional managed laptop displays an unfamiliar administrator account.
steps: Compare the account with the approved baseline and recent authorised support work.
Report the unexplained difference and follow the response procedure; do not assume a user’s name proves responsibility.

misconception.claim: A clean anti-malware scan proves a device is uncompromised.
misconception.correction: A scan has a detection scope and may miss unknown or hidden activity.

questions.prompt: Why avoid routine administrator access?
questions.hint: Consider the effect of mistakes or malicious software.
questions.answer: Least privilege limits the changes a normal session can make, reducing potential impact.
checkpoints: Does not claim all threats are prevented

questions.prompt: What should accompany a report of suspicious behaviour?
questions.hint: Record observable details.
questions.answer: The time, observed symptoms and relevant error or alert details, without altering or publicly exposing sensitive records.

questions.hint: Match permissions to the task.
questions.prompt: A student uses an administrator account for routine browsing. Explain the least-privilege concern and a suitable administrative remedy.
questions.answer: Routine browsing does not usually need broad administrative rights. An authorised administrator can provide a standard account for ordinary use and require elevated access only for approved tasks.
checkpoints: Explain the greater impact if the account or application is misused.
Suggest separated routine and approved elevated access.
hints: Match permissions to the task.
The remedy should preserve legitimate administration without giving it to every activity.

questions.hint: Check whether this exact change was expected.
questions.prompt: A device reports an unexpected configuration change immediately after a scheduled update. What should a reviewer compare before classifying it as an incident?
questions.answer: Compare the observed change with the approved update scope, change record and baseline version; timing is relevant but does not by itself prove either legitimacy or compromise.
checkpoints: Compare it with authorised change evidence.
Avoid treating timing alone as a definitive explanation.
hints: Check whether this exact change was expected.
Preserve the evidence even while a benign explanation is investigated.

notes.title: Reasoning through use a device baseline and safe response
paragraphs: A managed-device baseline records expected software, accounts, settings and update status so deviations can be investigated consistently. A difference is evidence to assess, not automatic proof of compromise: an approved update or administrative change may explain it. Least privilege reduces the actions available to ordinary accounts and limits consequences if those accounts are misused. A response should follow the organisation’s process, preserve relevant observations and avoid improvised deletion that destroys evidence. Record what was seen, when, where and under which account, then let authorised responders decide containment and recovery steps appropriate to the situation.

workedExamples.prompt: A fictional laptop baseline lists two administrator accounts, but a review finds three. The third was created yesterday and has no matching change record. Describe a proportionate first response.
steps: Record the unexpected account identifier, timestamps and relevant baseline comparison, and check the approved change process without using the account.
Report the unexplained deviation to the authorised support or incident team; preserve logs and follow their containment instructions.
workedExamples.conclusion: The evidence supports investigation of an unexplained privileged account, not an immediate conclusion about its origin.

flashcards.back: A recorded expected configuration used for comparison.
Grant only the access needed for the authorised task.

flashcards.front: Does every configuration change prove compromise?
flashcards.back: No; authorised changes may explain it.

flashcards.front: Why avoid deleting suspicious records immediately?
flashcards.back: Deletion can destroy evidence needed for investigation.

nodes.label: Expected baseline
nodes.detail: Record approved accounts, software and settings.

nodes.label: Observed deviation

nodes.label: Authorised response
nodes.detail: Verify change records, preserve evidence and escalate through the agreed process.

modules.title: Protect data and interpret access evidence
modules.focus: Unit 5: distinguish encryption, hashing and permission checks.
explanation: Encryption protects confidentiality by making data unreadable without the appropriate key. Hashing produces a digest useful for integrity checks and other constructions, but it does not provide reversible secrecy. Access controls decide which identities may read or change a resource and must be enforced at the relevant system boundary.

A safe review checks whether permissions match roles and whether logs record meaningful events. An unexpected access attempt may be an error or misuse; inspect context before concluding. Backups support recovery only when restoration has been tested under authorised procedures.

workedExample.prompt: A fictional class portal lets one learner request another learner’s private feedback.
steps: Identify an authorisation failure: the requested record belongs to a different user.
Require a server-side ownership or role check for each request and verify it with authorised test accounts; hiding the button alone is insufficient.

misconception.claim: Encrypting data removes the need for access controls.
misconception.correction: An authorised application can decrypt data, so it must still decide which user may receive it.

questions.prompt: Why is a hash not a substitute for encryption when secrecy and recovery are required?
questions.hint: Compare reversibility and purpose.
questions.answer: A hash is not designed to recover the original data; encryption supports recovery with a key while protecting confidentiality.

questions.prompt: Why test a backup restoration?
questions.hint: A stored copy alone is not the final outcome.
questions.answer: Testing checks whether the data and required configuration can actually be recovered in a usable form.
checkpoints: Does not assume success from file presence

questions.hint: A comparison is only as trustworthy as its reference.
questions.prompt: A file’s hash matches an expected value downloaded from the same untrusted location as the file. Does this alone establish integrity against a malicious source?
questions.answer: No. The source could replace both file and expected hash. The expected digest needs an independently trusted origin or authenticated mechanism for the comparison to provide that assurance.
checkpoints: Recognise that both values can be controlled together.
Explain the missing trust in the reference digest.
Identify the need for a trusted or authenticated reference.
hints: A comparison is only as trustworthy as its reference.
Matching numbers do not establish who supplied them.

questions.hint: A readable backup may still fail to produce a working service.
questions.prompt: A backup job reports success, but no restoration has been attempted. What additional evidence is needed before claiming recovery readiness?
questions.answer: An authorised restoration test should verify that required records, access permissions and dependencies are recovered correctly within the relevant time and data-loss objectives.
checkpoints: Distinguish successful copying from successful recovery.
Verify restored data and usable permissions or dependencies.
Measure the required recovery timing and data coverage.
hints: A readable backup may still fail to produce a working service.
Test the actual recovery objective, not only the job status.

notes.title: Reasoning through protect data and interpret access evidence
paragraphs: Data protection combines confidentiality, integrity and availability. Encryption protects readable content from parties without the required key, while hashing produces a digest useful for integrity checks when the expected digest is trusted. A hash does not provide a reversible confidential copy. Access checks must bind the authenticated user to the particular record and action, including when an identifier in a request changes. Backups support availability only if they can be restored with the required data, permissions and timing. Retention and access should match legitimate needs, because collecting or keeping extra sensitive information increases the amount that must be protected.

workedExamples.prompt: A fictional portal authorises a learner once at login but returns any feedback record whose numeric identifier is requested. Identify the flaw and a defensive check.
steps: The request selects an object without verifying that the current learner is allowed to access that object.
Each retrieval must check the authenticated identity’s permission for the requested record and action, returning no private data when permission is absent.
workedExamples.conclusion: The missing control is per-record authorisation, which must be enforced on the server for each request.

flashcards.back: Information from unauthorised disclosure.
Information from unauthorised or undetected alteration.
A digest is not a reversible protected copy of the original data.

flashcards.front: What proves a backup is usable?
flashcards.back: A successful authorised restoration test meeting the required scope and timing.
